hook.text: A loaded combine weighs 30 tons. Every pass crushes the soil beneath it—sometimes permanently.

buildup.text: Compacted soil has smaller pores, less air, and resists root penetration. Crops grow stunted.

discovery.text: Compaction layers can form deep underground—hardpan—blocking water drainage and trapping roots above.

twist.text: Wet soil compacts far more easily than dry soil. One pass on a wet field does years of damage.

climax.text: Controlled traffic farming—always driving on the same tracks—limits compaction to narrow strips.

punchline.text: Heavy machines make heavy problems. Stay off wet fields.

quiz.question: When does soil compact most easily?
options: When wet—one pass on saturated soil causes years of damage

details.summary: Soil compaction occurs when heavy equipment, livestock, or foot traffic compresses soil, destroying pore space essential for root growth, water infiltration, and aeration. This topic covers how compaction happens, how to diagnose it, and strategies for prevention and remediation.
details.whyItMatters: Compaction affects an estimated 68 million hectares of farmland in Europe alone. It can reduce crop yields by 10-20% and persists for decades in subsoil. Prevention is far more effective and cheaper than remediation.
takeaways: Heavy machinery creates compaction layers at 15-50 cm depth that persist for decades
Compacted soil reduces water infiltration by up to 80% and restricts root penetration
Controlled traffic farming confines machinery to permanent lanes to protect soil structure

faq.question: How can farmers diagnose soil compaction in their fields?
faq.answer: A penetrometer measures resistance to probe insertion—readings above 300 psi indicate compaction. Visible signs include poor water infiltration (ponding), stunted roots that bend horizontally, and poor crop growth in traffic lanes. Digging a soil pit reveals dense layers with no visible pores.

faq.question: What is the best way to remediate compacted soil?
faq.answer: Prevention is cheapest—using controlled traffic, reducing machinery weight, and avoiding wet-field operations. For existing compaction, deep-rooted cover crops like tillage radish slowly break up plow pans.
